::: notes
**$n + 1$.** Count it: the picture has 6 nodes and 7 null pointers.

Proof: there are $2n$ pointer fields in all. Every node except the root has
exactly one pointer aimed at it, so $n - 1$ of them are used. That leaves
$2n - (n - 1) = n + 1$ null.
:::

## Practice 1 {.smaller}

1) Draw a FULL tree with 9 nodes. Is it the same as your neighbour's?

::: notes
Give them a minute with a neighbour. It needn't be the same — there are several full
binary trees with 9 nodes. Every one has **4 internal nodes and 5 leaves**,
though: in a full binary tree, leaves = internal + 1.
:::

## Practice 2 {.smaller}

2) Draw a COMPLETE tree with 12 nodes. Is it the same as your neighbour's?

::: notes
This time it **is** the same as your neighbour's: a complete tree's shape is
fixed by its size. Levels of 1, 2, 4, and then 5 nodes on the bottom level,
filled from the left.
:::

## Practice 3 {.smaller}

3a) Give an *upper bound* for the number of nodes in a tree of height h:

\

\

3b) Give a *lower bound* for the height of a tree containing n nodes:

::: notes
3a) At most a perfect tree: $n \le 2^{h+1} - 1$.

3b) Turn it around: $2^{h+1} \ge n + 1$, so
$h \ge \log_2(n+1) - 1$. A binary tree with $n$ nodes has height
$\Omega(\log n)$ — this will matter for every search tree we build.
:::

## Practice 4 {.smaller}

4) Give upper and lower bounds for the number of nodes in a complete tree of
height h:

::: notes
**Most:** a perfect tree of height $h$, $2^{h+1} - 1$.

**Fewest:** a perfect tree of height $h-1$ plus one node starting the next
level: $(2^h - 1) + 1 = 2^h$.

So $2^h \le n \le 2^{h+1} - 1$, and a complete tree's height is exactly
$\lfloor \log_2 n \rfloor$.
:::

<text class="val" x="360" y="136.5" font-size="17" text-anchor="middle">e</text>
</g>
</svg>

::: notes
Every node, exactly once — in what order? On this expression tree the
three classic orders give three classic notations:

- **pre**order: `+ - / b c * d e` (prefix)
- **in**order: `- b / c + d * e` (infix — the expression as written)
- **post**order: `b c / - d e * +` (postfix, a stack machine's order)

The `-` has only a right child here: it's a unary minus.
:::

## {background-iframe="viz/traversal_tour.html" background-interactive="true"}

::: notes
Click into it first. **1 / 2 / 3** pick pre / in / post, **P** plays, **→**
steps, **T** changes tree, **R** resets.

The pointer passes every node three times — left side, underneath, right
side. Pick a pass and the node squawks there. Same walk, three orders: the
only thing that changes is *when you speak up*. That's the one line that
moves in the code.

Ask before playing: on the a–j tree, which letter squawks third in inorder?
(f: d, b, f…)
:::

::: notes
The given order is **in**order: 3, 12, 9, 7, 10, 15, 30, 20, 8.

- **Pre**order: 10, 12, 3, 9, 7, 15, 20, 30, 8
- **Post**order: 3, 7, 9, 12, 30, 8, 20, 15, 10

The code: one line, `visit(croot)` (say, `cout << croot->data`), goes in one
of three places — before both calls (pre), between them (in), or after both
(post). Same skeleton, three traversals.

Running time: each node is visited once, so $\Theta(n)$. (The proof is
next lecture.)

RT:
:::
::: {.column width="50%"}
```cpp
template<class T>
void tree<T>::__________(Node * croot) {
    if (croot != nullptr) {
        __________(croot->left);
        __________(croot->right);
        delete croot;
        croot = nullptr;
    }
}
```
:::
::::

::: notes
It deletes both subtrees, then the node: **a postorder traversal** that
frees the whole tree — call it `clear` or `destroy`. It has to be post:
delete the node first and `croot->left` is gone.

RT: $\Theta(n)$, one visit per node.

Look at the last line: `croot` is a *copy* of the caller's pointer, so
setting it to `nullptr` changes nothing outside. The caller's `root` still
points at freed memory. Fix: take `Node *& croot`.
:::

```cpp
template<class T>
Node * tree<T>::copy(Node * croot) {








}
```
:::
::::

::: notes
```
if (croot == nullptr) return nullptr;
Node * t = new Node(croot->data);
t->left  = copy(croot->left);
t->right = copy(croot->right);
return t;
```

Make the node first, then its subtrees: a **pre**order traversal. (Building
the children first and the node last — postorder — works too.) Traversal is
a pattern for *any* whole-tree job, not just printing.
:::
